extracted.intended_audience: aerospace and cryogenic engineers, NASA technical staff, and researchers studying thermal-acoustic oscillations in cryogenic storage systems
extracted.subtask_description: Technical-report–style experimental study and model correlation of thermally driven acoustic oscillations in a supercritical hydrogen spherical tank, including data reduction, comparison to Rott/Liburdy analytical models, and hardware mitigation trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units and conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: All data are presented in the International System of Units as the primary system and English units as the secondary system. All calculations were done in English units and converted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report primary results in SI, include secondary English units; if calculations are performed in other units, show conversions. Consistent unit reporting is necessary for comparing test data with analytical models and literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum data fields for reduced test table (Table 3-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table 3-1 contains the test purpose, configuration correlated to Figures 2-1 through 2-17, line (supply, fill or vent), environmental temperature, internal tank temperature, and oscillation frequency and amplitude. Acoustic velocity (a) and kinematic viscosity (v) for the internal tank temperature are given. The thermal acoustic oscillation parameter Y* (defined as r^ (ω/ν)^(1/2) ) has been calculated for all data points. Notes indicate valve positions and secondary modes (secondary frequency and amplitude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reducing experimental runs, include these fields for each data point so they can be used directly for model correlation; mark valve positions and secondary modes explicitly to aid interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document hardware configurations and external flow diagrams with line lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventeen hardware configurations were identified and examined; Figures 2-1 through 2-17 contain the external flow diagrams for the 17 different configurations. Line lengths are given in Figure 2-1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide schematic flow diagrams and explicit line length measurements for every hardware configuration tested; these are required to compute nondimensional length ratios and select appropriate analytical stability curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record temperature profile of fluid lines (instrumentation requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data contains no information as to the temperature profile (a function of distance from the pressure vessel to the outer vacuum shell). Determining hot and cold fluid line lengths required for comparison with analytical models is a difficult task for a production cryogenic tank due to insufficient data on the line's temperature profile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrument and record temperature as a function of distance along lines (hot and cold lengths and gradient steepness) during testing; without these measurements cold-length estimates and model correlations are highly uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient variation of operating conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The operating conditions do not vary sufficiently to allow determination of the effect of varying temperature ratios on the stability limit. The ratio of hot to cold temperatures only vary from 7.0 to 12.2, while flow rates varied in general from 0 kg/sec to 1.7 kg/sec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tests to span a wider range of temperature ratios and flow rates to permit meaningful evaluation of analytical stability predictions; limited parameter variance impedes verification of models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate waterhammer transients from thermal-acoustic steady oscillations
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening or closing a valve generates a change in the fluid velocity from the steady state condition. This velocity change is accompanied by a pressure change proportional to the velocity change (waterhammer). This pressure transient, which travels at the acoustic velocity of the fluid, is damped by viscous forces. This pressure perturbation was, in most cases, followed by the steady pressure oscillations attributed to thermal acoustic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing pressure traces, identify and exclude or separately document valve-induced transient (waterhammer) events before attributing subsequent signals to thermally sustained acoustic oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record valve positions and note perturbation events
rubrics_metrics.description: Table 3-1 contains notes indicating valve positions. Small perturbations (for example, opening MV-525) can initiate oscillations; valve position changes are correlated with the appearance or disappearance of oscillations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log valve positions, timing of adjustments, and any perturbation events with timestamps synchronized to pressure traces to permit cause-effect analysis of oscillation onsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and test line restrictions and insulation as hardware mitigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rockwell personnel tried insulating flow lines and tank surfaces; various insulation systems were tried but no significant positive results could be observed. Restrictions in the lines (washer-type orifices) were installed in various locations; some orifices made filling impossible. The most successful restriction appeared to be a 2.39 mm (0.173 in.) diameter orifice in the fill line close to the tank interface, but this was not a definite solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically test insulation and a range of orifice sizes/locations, documenting effects on oscillation frequency/amplitude and operational consequences (e.g., ability to fill). Avoid orifices that prevent required flow; report both effectiveness and operational trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute nondimensional parameters for model comparison (Y*, X, §, frequency parameters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermal acoustic oscillation parameter Y* (r^ (ω/ν)^(1/2)) and frequency parameters X and Y are used in the analytical models; nondimensional length § = (L-1)/1 and other nondimensional groups are central to Rott's stability curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate and report all relevant nondimensional parameters (Y*, X, §, nondimensional frequency, nondimensional mean flow F) for each data point to allow plotting against analytical stability curves and asymptotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select accurate thermophysical property values for supercritical hydrogen (β, γ, Pr)
rubrics_metrics.description: The properties of supercritical hydrogen present problems in determining the appropriate values for the Prandtl number, the ratio of specific heats and the exponent for the power law viscosity curve used in the analytical model. For this study the following values were used for hydrogen at 1.9 MPa: β = 0.823, γ = 1.42 and Pr = 0.71.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine and justify property values at the operating pressure/temperature range (show sensitivity of model predictions to β, γ, and Pr). For supercritical fluids, properties may vary strongly with temperature—report the chosen values and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify long-tube assumption before applying Rott's analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Rott's analysis is based on the long tube constraint which requires the tube length to be much larger than the tube radius. The PRSA Hydrogen Tank lines have effective length-to-diameter (L/D) ratios of approximately 50, 130 and 150 for the vent, fill and supply lines, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm L/D >> 1 (quantify L/D) for the lines in question; only then apply Rott's long-tube-based analytical solutions. If the assumption is marginal, note its effect on applicability of the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess temperature-profile steepness versus idealized jump assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Rott's models idealize the temperature profile as two constant temperature sections joined by a temperature jump where dT/dx is infinite. The relatively low steepness of the temperature jump existing in the PRSA fluid lines increases the uncertainty in predicting the stability limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the temperature-profile steepness (as per Eq. 4-1) and evaluate whether the idealized discontinuous jump assumption is valid; if not, account for nonideal gradients in analysis or note increased uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to include mean-flow term (Liburdy) versus zero-flow Rott model
rubrics_metrics.description: Liburdy added a net flow term to Rott's analysis; for this study nondimensional mean flow F ranged up to ~28 and, for the relatively low temperature ratios and Y* values, the effect of Liburdy's mean flow term was negligible. Based on this, the decision was made to use Rott's analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute nondimensional mean flow F = (mean flow velocity)/(cold-end acoustic velocity) for test conditions; include the mean-flow term in analytical comparisons if F and parameter ranges indicate nonnegligible effect (especially for upper-branch regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate cold and hot lengths to select correct stability curve parameter (§)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of which curve (value of §) the correlation should be made on requires a determination of the hot-to-cold length ratio §. If the fluid-line interface with the outer shell is assumed a thermal short, the maximum cold length is one-half the effective line length. For the fill and vent lines this is 1.9 m and 0.9 m respectively; supply-line cold length approximated as ~8.0 m. Values of § between 1 and 10 are reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate cold-length and hot-length (with instrumentation if possible) and use these to pick the stability-curve (§) for correlation; if uncertain, evaluate sensitivity across a plausible § range (e.g., 1–10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report experimental limitations and plan future targeted testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions identify limitations: supercritical hydrogen properties yield poor agreement with constant Pr and power-law viscosity; lack of instrumentation prevented determination of actual cold fluid line lengths; small steepness ratio questions validity of discontinuous temperature jump; small parameter variation prevents definitive verification of analytical models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting, explicitly list limitations that affect model correlation and recommend future work: instrumented dewar studies (subcritical and supercritical hydrogen), more extensive parameter sweeps, and experiments designed to study nonideal conditions to provide design data for production tanks.
